articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Bring an Iced Coffee to a Job Interview?
articles.content:
It was the iced latte that broke the internet: In a now-infamous TikTok, recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen, said she’s noticed Gen Z job candidates showing up to interviews with an iced latte in hand—which, she argued, made it seem less like a professional career moment and more like stop No. 5 on the candidate’s errand list, somewhere between Starbucks and Target.
The internet, naturally, lost its mind over this anecdote. The debate split pretty cleanly along generational lines. Older people saw the drink and thought, Pshaw! We used to go to interviews in our best suits, with our résumés printed on actual paper. Younger people saw the same coffee and thought, OK? And? Others pointed out that maybe the bigger story wasn’t the beverage but the job market, where getting an entry-level job increasingly feels like applying to become an astronaut.
All of which raises the question: Is it actually rude to bring an iced coffee—or tea or water bottle—into a job interview?
Admit it: You had an immediate gut reaction the second you read that question. As did I. There’s something about the image of an artfully poured coffee in an interview that feels either inappropriately bougie or completely innocuous, depending on how many years you’ve spent being told to “dress for the job you want.”
But as a Millennial, I have the rare privilege of being able to be in this generational battle with very low stakes. I’m just glad that for once no one is yelling at us. I’m not here to referee TikTok, settle the beverage wars between Gen Z vs. everyone else, or confiscate anyone’s Stanley. I’m here to render an etiquette verdict. So let’s do it.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, career, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
“It’s taking care of a basic need. I don’t see what the big deal is,” says Rebecca M., a former hiring manager for several large companies who has sat in on hundreds of job interviews. And really, that’s the basis of most of the “go for it” arguments: Humans drink things. “Am I allowed to admit this? I always bring my water bottle. Hydration is very important!” she says. “So maybe I need extra water to be my best self, and maybe they need extra caffeine.”
Plus, for many people, holding a coffee calms their nerves and gives them something to do with their hands. “It’s one reason why we so often offer a drink to candidates,” she adds. “We want them to feel comfortable.”
And, most importantly, it does not say anything about the person’s ability to do the job. Unless the job is making coffee. Then I suppose it could be gauche to bring in a rival barista’s work.
But there is a more subtle reason some people are doing this: a tiny bit of rebellion. Older generations have set the workplace norms for decades, and some of these norms have made basic human needs considerably more complicated than necessary. Think: high heels for walking, three-piece suits in the summer and a devotion to email that feels almost cultlike.
Norms change. That’s how norms work. “I have heard of this, but mostly as a ‘haha, boomers are so sensitive’ thing,” says Nav A., a Gen Zer who graduated in May and just landed his first job. (Congrats!) Did he bring a drink to his interview? “I always bring a water bottle. It never occurred to me not to,” he says. “For me, it’s such a small thing that if the interviewer has an issue with it, that’s a big red flag that maybe this isn’t somewhere I want to work.”
It’s less about the iced latte and more about what the iced latte communicates. Are you taking this seriously? Do you really want this job? Or is this just something to check off on your to-do list?
First impressions form fast. “Unfortunately, Gen Z is already seen as fragile, oblivious, self-centered and unprepared, and bringing a fancy coffee may reinforce that stereotype,” says Brandon P., a Gen X manager at a tech company who hires a lot of younger people. To be clear, he doesn’t agree with the stereotype and says some of his best workers are Gen Z. “But I’ll be honest: I would think the person was unprofessional. It’s not the worst mistake, but when every little thing counts in a first impression, I’d avoid anything that might bias the interviewer against you.”
And that’s the real issue: You have no idea who is sitting across from you. The interviewer might be completely unfazed by your almond-milk pumpkin-spice cold brew. They might even think it’s adorable! They might barely register it. Or they might spend the first five minutes of the interview wondering why you couldn’t go 45 minutes without caffeine. Some people might be enraged by it. Or, says Rebecca, they might have misophonia, a common condition that makes people extra sensitive to noises like drinking or slurping.
Then there’s logistics. While holding a cup may comfort you, spilling it all over your lap, the carpet or (heaven forbid) the interviewer is unlikely to improve your chances of getting hired. Is this common? No. But there’s zero chance of this happening if you’re just not holding a drink in the first place. Plus, those iced drinks always form condensation on the outside, which makes them wet and drippy. Then, when the interviewer goes to shake your hand, you’ll only have one hand free, and it might be … moist. Ugh.
There’s also the matter of how you drink it. “I wouldn’t say a drink itself is rude, but I sure have seen people drink it in a very rude way,” Rebecca says. Slurping. Chewing ice. Stirring it noisily. Aggressively crinkling the plastic cup. Leaving drips, napkins, stirrers or the entire beverage behind for someone else to clean up.
But at that point, the problem isn’t that the coffee is rude—it’s that you are rude.
Not everything is cut and dried (and then added to an herbal tea blend). A lot of good etiquette depends on how you do it. Here are a few factors to consider when deciding whether your beverage should ride along for your interview.
No, it’s not rude to bring an iced coffee to a job interview … but it’s also not risk-free. There’s an important distinction between rude and strategically smart. A drink doesn’t automatically communicate disrespect, laziness or a lack of interest in the job. Plenty of perfectly professional adults drink coffee all day long. But if you’re interviewing somewhere formal, you don’t know the interviewer or you’re already nervous about making a good impression, there’s very little to gain from arriving with a giant iced coffee.
“If you’re not sure if it’s OK, err on the side of safety,” Brandon says. “No one has ever not gotten a job because they didn’t bring in an iced latte.”
And there is a very simple solution: You don’t have to pretend your caffeine addiction doesn’t exist. You can simply finish drinking the coffee before you walk through the door.
At the end of the day, though, I suspect this whole debate may be one of those internet tempests in a teapot. Not one person I talked to had actually witnessed an iced-coffee interview scandal in the wild. And while most agreed they wouldn’t bring a specialty coffee into an interview themselves, they also said they wouldn’t be particularly offended if someone else did.
So perhaps we can all agree that the latte is not the real problem here. There are bigger etiquette questions to fight about, like whether “no problem” is an acceptable response to “thank you” and how many times you can double-text someone before it officially becomes a situation.

articles.title: The Nicest Moments of 2026—So Far! (Warning: You Might Get a Little Emotional)
articles.content:
If 2026 has taught us anything, it’s that life can be a lot. The headlines have been exhausting, and the world has felt especially heavy. But mixed in with all of that have been some beautiful, surprising moments that remind us there’s still plenty of good happening too. The nicest moments have a habit of sneaking up on you like that, usually when you least expect them and sometimes when you need them most.
So we wanted to give those moments the attention they deserve. From a flight attendant who helped a tired mom to runners who sacrificed their own finish times to astronauts who know the true meaning of friendship, the acts of kindness in this story will give you a little break from everything else going on—and help you remember that good people are still out there doing really good things.
Read on for the heartwarming moments that have made 2026 a little brighter.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
In late March, Boise pizza delivery driver Dan Simpson learned his Domino’s location had run out of the Diet Coke a customer had ordered. Rather than arrive empty-handed, the 68-year-old stopped at a convenience store and bought the drinks himself. The small gesture was caught on the customer’s Ring camera and went viral—and when people learned Simpson was preparing to retire after 14 years of delivering pizzas, they returned the kindness in a big way. More than 8,000 people contributed $170,000 to a fundraiser for his retirement, allowing “Dan the Man” to officially hang up his delivery bag in May.
During a shift in August, a Wendy’s employee named Dara approached Florida homeowner Abigail Mwaungulu with an unusual request: Could she spend her lunch break on the porch? Mwaungulu said yes, and her Ring camera captured the beginning of a new friendship. As more of Dara’s story came to light—including the fact that she walks to work every day—people watching online wanted to do something for her too. They started a fundraiser that has since brought in more than $17,000 to help with Dara’s transportation, education and whatever she may need for what comes next.
On Sept. 2, Republic Airways flight attendant Monique Harris noticed an exhausted mother nodding off with her baby on a flight from Newark to Grand Rapids, Michigan. When the baby began slipping from the mother’s lap, Harris quickly caught him and offered to hold him while Mom got some much-needed sleep. Another person on the plane snapped a photo of the tender moment, which went viral on Instagram, earning more than 200,000 likes within days.
About 1,000 feet from the end of the Boston Marathon in April, American Ajay Haridasse stumbled and fell. Seeing him on the ground, two other runners, Aaron Beggs of Northern Ireland and Robson De Oliveira of Brazil, helped him up, sacrificing their own personal best times to do so. Each draped one of Haridasse’s arms over their shoulders to carry him the rest of the way and across the finish line.
Fans of Catherine O’Hara were heartbroken when the beloved comedy icon died in January. Then in March, she posthumously won an Actor Award for her work on the sitcom The Studio. Showrunner Seth Rogen accepted on her behalf, and in his speech, Rogen said of his friend and co-star, “She really showed that you can be a genius and be kind, and one of those things does not have to come at the expense of the other.”
American figure skater Ilia Malinin (aka the “Quad God”) was the heavy favorite to win the men’s singles competition at the Winter Olympic Games in Milano Cortina in February. But during his free skate performance, Malinin fell twice and finished well outside of medal contention. Despite his disappointment, Malinin was the first to congratulate the gold medal winner, Mikhail Shaidorov of Kazakhstan. His show of sportsmanship earned him the Fair Play Award, an international prize voted on by the public, after a record-breaking number of votes cast by fans worldwide.
The world watched as the Artemis II astronauts made their 10-day trek around the moon in April. Their journey took them farther from Earth than humans had ever been, making them the first to see certain parts of the far side of the moon. This meant that they also got to propose names for two previously undiscovered craters, and for one of them, they chose to honor the late wife of their commander, Reid Wiseman.
In a video message to Mission Control, an audibly emotional Jeremy Hansen described the crater as “a bright spot on the moon” before saying, “We would like to call it Carroll.” As Hansen spoke, his fellow crew members were seen dabbing at their eyes. Then the four astronauts floated toward one another and embraced in a zero-gravity hug.
While presenting an award at the Academy of Country Music Awards in May, Shania Twain and Shaboozey asked the audience at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas to join them in wishing Willie Nelson a happy birthday. Nelson, who wasn’t in attendance that night, had just turned 93, and an arena full of country music fans wanted the legendary singer/songwriter to feel the love. So in unison, they shouted, “Happy birthday, Willie!” while Shaboozey recorded the moment on his phone to send to the star.
After a decade on the air, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert came to a close in May. Leading up to the last show, many of Colbert’s famous friends stopped by the Ed Sullivan Theater to say goodbye, including fellow late-night hosts Jimmy Fallon, Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers and John Oliver. The quintet appeared all together at one of Colbert’s final tapings, and both Kimmel and Fallon (whose time slots coincided with Colbert’s) aired reruns the night of his send-off so as not to compete with their friend’s farewell.
As the FIFA World Cup got underway in June, Japanese soccer fans went viral for how they helped clean up after games, filling blue garbage bags with other people’s trash on their way out of Texas Stadium in Dallas and Estadio Monterrey in Mexico. “We are honored to be here,” one fan explained to USA Today. “So we don’t want to make a mess and then leave it.”

articles.title: 5 Ways You Can Become a Morning Person (Yes, Even If You’re a Night Owl!)
articles.content:
It isn’t easy to wake up early. And if you’re not a morning person? That’s a whole other level of misery.
Now, let me put this out there first: If you’re a night owl, you’re not being lazy. Some of us just aren’t hardwired to be at our peak in the a.m. I’ll admit I need at least three cups of coffee in the morning for my brain to come online. And you’ll never catch me at the gym before work.

articles.content:
Carrie Bradshaw had us believing that high heels were appropriate for just about everything—cocktail parties, first dates, running around Manhattan and, heck, probably a quick grocery-store run too. And even if sky-high stilettos aren’t your thing, there’s something about slipping into a good, old-fashioned kitten heel that can make an ordinary Tuesday feel a little more fabulous. (Your feet may have some thoughts a few hours later, but that’s another story.) Yet for all the glamour and wobbling over cobblestones those shoes have given us, the history of high heels is a lot more surprising than you might expect. For starters, they weren’t even originally made for women. Yes, really!
So how did high heels become a fashion statement and a fixture in women’s closets? And after centuries of being revered, are they on their way out? To get to the bottom of it all, we spoke with Elizabeth Semmelhack, director and senior curator at the Bata Shoe Museum in Toronto, Canada.
Read on to learn how high heels climbed to the top of the fashion world—and whether they’re about to come back down to earth.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more history, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
There’s no single inventor we can credit with the high heel, or even an exact date when heels first appeared. What we do know is that they’ve been around for at least 1,000 years and were first worn by men. Their original purpose was all about function, not fashion, and they were mainly used in—get this—horseback riding! (More on that below.) Over the centuries, heels shifted in shape, height and meaning, moving between men’s and women’s wardrobes along the way.
High heels have taken a surprisingly winding path from practical footwear to status symbol to fashion staple. Here’s the fascinating history behind high heels.
The earliest known heels weren’t designed for walking—they were made for riding. “They were worn as far back as the 10th century in Persia as an equestrian tool used in tandem with the stirrup,” says Semmelhack. “This is why cowboys still wear heels.”
Worn mostly by male riders, they were sturdy and practical, with a chunky, block-shaped heel roughly an inch high. That little bit of height was enough to hook the foot more securely into the stirrup. Plus, the shoes themselves were made from tough animal leather, making them easier to withstand riding and harsh outdoor conditions.
By the 16th century, heels were beginning to take on a very different life in Europe. One of the most famous stories from this period of history involves Catherine de’ Medici. When the Italian noblewoman married the Duke of Orléans—the future Henry II of France—in 1533, she was just 14 years old. According to a story that has been repeated for generations, the petite Catherine had specially made heeled shoes created for the wedding to give her some extra height and presence when she arrived at the French court.
It’s a great story, but there’s a catch: Historians have questioned whether Catherine really introduced high heels to France this way, and there isn’t strong evidence to confirm the tale. What her story does show, though, is how closely heels would eventually become tied to European court life and appearance.
By the following century, that connection was much clearer … but men were at the center of it. “Heels entered Western fashion around the turn of the 17th century, with Northern European men adding them to their riding boots first,” Semmelhack says. “Over the course of the 17th century, men throughout Europe began to wear heels for fashion as well.”
And these weren’t men just trying to sneak an extra inch into their shoes. Heels became a real fashion statement, especially in Europe’s royal circles. Louis XIV of France is probably one of the most famous examples. He was known for wearing red heels, a style that became closely associated with his court. England’s Charles II got in on the trend too. A portrait from around 1675 to 1680 shows him wearing square-toed shoes with bright red heels.
“Heels were abandoned in men’s fashion for reasons associated with shifting ideas of gender in the 18th century,” Semmelhack says. “Men, it was suggested, were ‘rational,’ and men’s fashion changed to support this new idea of manliness that included the loss of the high heel. Women were positioned as ‘irrational,’ and heels off the horse are arguably impractical, so they became associated with both female irrationality and female desirability.”
Men didn’t abandon every kind of heel, though. Look at a classic brogue, and you’ll still find a small stacked heel, while cowboy and riding boots have more substantial ones. Plus, higher heels are still seen in men’s fashion, including in nightlife and contemporary designer collections.
According to Semmelhack, “the biggest innovation in heels came when steel started to be used to make extremely thin stilettos in the early 1950s.” And designers ran with it. One of the biggest names was French shoe designer Roger Vivier, often called the “father of the stiletto.” While designing shoes for Christian Dior in the 1950s, Vivier became known for treating the heel almost like a piece of architecture, experimenting with new shapes and silhouettes rather than simply changing its height.
Among the designs most closely associated with him was the Aiguille heel. Aiguille means “needle” in French, and the name tells you pretty much everything you need to know. It was incredibly slender and sharply tapered, creating the kind of delicate, needle-thin silhouette that helped define the modern stiletto. Vivier would go on to experiment with other distinctive shapes too, including curved and sculptural heels, helping turn the heel itself into part of the design rather than something simply holding up the back of a shoe.
Then Carrie Bradshaw took that obsession to another level. When Sex and the City debuted in 1998, Carrie’s designer heels became almost as memorable as her dating life. Manolo Blahniks weren’t just sitting quietly in her closet either. They made their way into storylines about money, relationships and even marriage, helping turn the designer heel into both a fashion statement and a pop-culture phenomenon. By the early 2000s, a pair of stilettos could be something to save up for, obsess over and plan an entire outfit around.
Heels aren’t disappearing, but they have a lot more competition these days. Comfort-first dressing got a major boost during the pandemic, when commutes and nights out suddenly disappeared for millions of people. Flats, sneakers and other easy-to-wear shoes had a moment, and they didn’t exactly vanish once everyone started going out again.
Still, don’t count heels out. “I have been asking myself this question a lot lately,” Semmelhack says. “Heels are central to Republican constructs of femininity at the moment, but they are also having a resurgence in high fashion, where the sculptural possibilities of heels are being played with. It is an interesting moment in the history of the high heel.”
So high heels probably aren’t headed for the history books. After centuries of changing shape and even who wears them, they may simply be changing again.

What her story does show, though, is how closely heels would eventually become tied to European court life and appearance.

England’s Charles II got in on the trend too. A portrait from around 1675 to 1680 shows him wearing square-toed shoes with bright red heels.

Why did men stop wearing high heels?

“Heels were abandoned in men’s fashion for reasons associated with shifting ideas of gender in the 18th century,” Semmelhack says. “Men, it was suggested, were ‘rational,’ and men’s fashion changed to support this new idea of manliness that included the loss of the high heel. Men didn’t abandon every kind of heel, though. Look at a classic brogue, and you’ll still find a small stacked heel, while cowboy and riding boots have more substantial ones. Plus, higher heels are still seen in men’s fashion, including in nightlife and contemporary designer collections.

When did heels become the women’s shoes we know, love and sometimes hate today?

According to Semmelhack, “the biggest innovation in heels came when steel started to be used to make extremely thin stilettos in the early 1950s.” And designers ran with it. One of the biggest names was French shoe designer Roger Vivier, often called the “father of the stiletto.” While designing shoes for Christian Dior in the 1950s, Vivier became known for treating the heel almost like a piece of architecture, experimenting with new shapes and silhouettes rather than simply changing its height.

Among the designs most closely associated with him was the Aiguille heel. Aiguille means “needle” in French, and the name tells you pretty much everything you need to know. It was incredibly slender and sharply tapered, creating the kind of delicate, needle-thin silhouette that helped define the modern stiletto. Vivier would go on to experiment with other distinctive shapes too, including curved and sculptural heels, helping turn the heel itself into part of the design rather than something simply holding up the back of a shoe.

Then Carrie Bradshaw took that obsession to another level. When Sex and the City debuted in 1998, Carrie’s designer heels became almost as memorable as her dating life. Manolo Blahniks weren’t just sitting quietly in her closet either. They made their way into storylines about money, relationships and even marriage, helping turn the designer heel into both a fashion statement and a pop-culture phenomenon. By the early 2000s, a pair of stilettos could be something to save up for, obsess over and plan an entire outfit around.

Are heels on their way out?

Heels aren’t disappearing, but they have a lot more competition these days. Comfort-first dressing got a major boost during the pandemic, when commutes and nights out suddenly disappeared for millions of people. Flats, sneakers and other easy-to-wear shoes had a moment, and they didn’t exactly vanish once everyone started going out again.

Still, don’t count heels out. “I have been asking myself this question a lot lately,” Semmelhack says. “Heels are central to Republican constructs of femininity at the moment, but they are also having a resurgence in high fashion, where the sculptural possibilities of heels are being played with. It is an interesting moment in the history of the high heel.”

So high heels probably aren’t headed for the history books. After centuries of changing shape and even who wears them, they may simply be changing again.

Look around for a “should.” You should have this kind of career. You should spend weekends this way. You should own a house by a certain age. You should have a particular kind of relationship. Then ask yourself who made that rule.

At work, experiment with technology or a new system that eliminates something tedious. If your schedule isn’t working, rearrange it. In your social life, seek out people who share your interests rather than maintaining friendships solely because you’ve known someone forever.

Aquarius is also associated with groups and community, so if you’ve become isolated, join something. Volunteer for a cause, find a local organization or seek out people who are fascinated by the same wonderfully obscure thing you are.

Just don’t rebel for the sake of rebellion. A conventional solution isn’t automatically a bad one. Keep the rules that work; toss the ones that don’t.

Pisces (Feb. 19–March 20)

Dreamy Pisces is imaginative, intuitive and creative. You can picture possibilities other people don’t see, which is an extraordinary gift. The adulting problem arrives when those possibilities remain beautiful little movies playing inside your head. Your reset is to make one dream concrete. Want to write a book? Set a weekly page goal. Dreaming of Paris? Open a vacation account and automatically deposit money into it every payday. Want a different career? Spend one hour this week researching what training you would actually need. Creativity becomes powerful when you give it a container.

Your environment matters too. Pisces absorbs atmosphere easily, so create spaces that help you feel calm and inspired. Music, water, art, meditation or simply taking a walk without your phone can help you clear out other people’s noise and hear your own thoughts again. And remember: Relationships require boundaries. Your empathy can make somebody else’s crisis feel like your responsibility. Before rushing in to rescue someone, ask whether they actually need your help and whether you genuinely have the energy to give it.

Your pitfall is waiting for inspiration, rescue or the perfect moment. Put one date on the calendar, and take one practical step. Dreams need feet.
